title: News Feed
brief: Design the home feed of a social app: a list of recent posts from the people you follow, newest first. People open it many times a day, so it must load fast. Some accounts have millions of followers, and one post from them must not melt the system.

functional: Publish a post with text and optional images.
Open a home feed of recent posts from people you follow.
Scroll back through older posts, a page at a time.
A deleted post disappears from every feed.

nonFunctional.name: Read latency
nonFunctional.target: The first page of the feed loads in under 200 ms at the 99th percentile

nonFunctional.name: Freshness
nonFunctional.target: A new post shows up in followers' feeds within 10 seconds

nonFunctional.name: Availability
nonFunctional.target: The feed loads 99.95% of the time, even if it is slightly stale

nonFunctional.name: Durability
nonFunctional.target: A published post is never lost

estimate.note: Reads dominate, and each post is copied into many feeds. The copy count (posts per second times followers) is the number that shapes the design. Assume 1 KB per stored post and one year of posts.

inputs.label: Feed opens per user per day
Bytes per feed entry
inputs.note: A post id and a timestamp.

outputs.label: Fan-out writes per second
outputs.note: Each post is pushed into every follower's feed list.

outputs.label: Writes for one celebrity post
outputs.note: A celebrity with 10M followers: one post, 10M list updates.

outputs.label: Feed reads per second
outputs.note: Peak is often 2 to 3 times this.

outputs.label: Feed cache memory
outputs.note: Upper bound: one list for every active user.

outputs.label: Post storage, one year
outputs.note: Text and metadata only. Images go to blob storage.

api.does: Stores a post and starts the fan-out. Returns the post id.
Marks the post deleted. Feeds drop it when they are read.
Returns the next page of post cards for the caller, newest first, plus a cursor.
Adds a follow edge. Unfollow is the matching DELETE.
Returns an upload URL. The image goes straight to blob storage.

data.fields: postId, authorId, text, mediaIds, createdAt, deleted
data.why: Reads are by id, so one lookup per post. Time-ordered ids help.
Both questions are common: who do I follow, and who follows me.

data.store: In-memory cache, a list per user.
data.why: The feed is precomputed. Opening it is one list read, trimmed to the newest N.
Small list per celebrity, read at feed time instead of fanned out.

evolution.title: One server, one query
evolution.problem: Start with what works: one server and one database holding posts and follows.
evolution.change: To build a feed, join the follows table to the posts table, sort by time and take the newest 20.

evolution.title: Precomputed feed cache
evolution.problem: Feeds are read about five times a day per user, and the join touches every person you follow. It gets slow as follows grow.
evolution.change: Keep a list of post ids per user in a cache. Opening the feed becomes one list read, then a lookup of those posts.
evolution.numbers: the estimator shows the cache is hundreds of GB

evolution.title: Fan-out on write
evolution.problem: Who fills the lists? Doing it inside the publish request makes posting slow and fragile.
evolution.change: A post is saved, then an event goes on a queue. Workers push the post id into each follower's list. This is fan-out on write: pay once at write time so reads stay cheap.
evolution.numbers: fan-out writes per second = posts per second times followers

evolution.title: A real follow store
evolution.problem: Workers need the follower list of an author at once, and the posts database also serves post reads.
evolution.change: Move follows into their own store, indexed both ways. Workers read followers from it. The post store stays focused on posts.

evolution.title: Media off to blob and CDN
evolution.problem: Images are far larger than text. Serving them through the app wastes servers and is slow far away.
evolution.change: Upload images to blob storage. A CDN, a cache of copies near the user, serves them. Posts only store media ids.

evolution.title: Hybrid for celebrities
evolution.problem: One post from an account with 10 million followers means 10 million list writes and a huge queue spike.
evolution.change: Do not fan out celebrities. Keep their recent posts in a small cache. When a feed is read, merge the ordinary list with the celebrity posts of the people you follow.
evolution.numbers: the celebrity line in the estimator

steps.say: The client sends the text and any image ids.
The service saves the post in the post store. From here it is durable.
It puts a new-post event on the queue and answers the client. It does not wait for fan-out.
The worker reads the author's followers. If the author is a celebrity it stops here.
For everyone else it pushes the post id onto each follower's list, trims the list, and skips inactive users.
A celebrity post instead goes into the small celebrity list. Nothing is copied.
The client asks for page one of the feed.
The service reads the user's id list from the feed cache. One lookup.
It also reads recent posts from the celebrities this user follows.
It merges both lists by time and keeps the newest page.
It hydrates the ids: fetches the post bodies and drops deleted ones.
The page goes back. Images load separately from the CDN.

deepDives.title: Fan-out on write, read or hybrid
deepDives.question: When do we build each person's feed: when a post is written, or when the feed is opened?

options.name: Fan-out on write (push)
options.pros: Reads are one list lookup. Fast and cheap for the common case.
options.cons: A post by a celebrity costs millions of writes. Work is wasted on users who never come back.

options.name: Fan-out on read (pull)
options.pros: Posting is one write. Nothing is wasted on inactive users.
options.cons: Every open queries everyone you follow and merges. Slow, and reads are the heavy side.

options.name: Hybrid
options.pros: Push for normal authors, pull only for celebrities. Both sides stay cheap.
options.cons: Two paths to build and test. Needs a rule for who counts as a celebrity.

deepDives.because: Reads vastly outnumber posts, so push by default. Few accounts have huge followings, so pulling just those at read time is a small merge. Pick the cutoff by follower count, for example 100K.

deepDives.title: Chronological or ranked
deepDives.question: Do we show posts newest first, or in the order a model thinks you will like?

options.name: Chronological
options.pros: Simple, predictable, cheap. The list is already in order.
options.cons: Busy follows bury the posts you care about.

options.name: Ranked in the fan-out
options.cons: Scores go stale, and changing the model means rewriting every list.

options.name: Ranked as a separate stage
options.pros: Fetch candidates cheaply, then score the top few hundred at read time. Models change without touching storage.
options.cons: Adds latency and a ranking service to run.

deepDives.because: Keep storage chronological and dumb. Candidate generation is the fan-out and merge. Ranking is a stage after it. You can ship, test or turn it off without rebuilding feeds.

deepDives.title: Inactive users and cache size
deepDives.question: Keeping a list for every user is expensive. Who deserves one?

options.name: A list for every account
options.pros: Every open is fast, even after a long absence.
options.cons: Most memory and writes go to people who never look.

options.name: Lists only for active users
options.pros: Memory and fan-out shrink a lot. Workers skip users not seen for 30 days.
options.cons: The first open after a long gap is slow.

options.name: Short lists with eviction
options.pros: Bounded size. Old entries drop off the end.
options.cons: Scrolling past the list needs a fallback to the post store.

deepDives.because: Skip fan-out for anyone who has not logged in for 30 days. On their next open, rebuild the list from the post store, then keep it warm. Trim each list to a few hundred entries, and read deeper pages from the post store.

failures.impact: New posts reach feeds late. Followers see stale feeds.
failures.fix: Scale workers with queue depth. Spread work by follower id, so no single worker owns a huge list. Alert on queue age, not just size.

failures.impact: Every list is gone. Opens would fall back to slow joins.
failures.fix: Rebuild a user's list on demand from the post store and follow store, newest first. Limit how many rebuilds run at once and warm the most active users first.

failures.what: A celebrity posts at peak time
failures.impact: A burst of reads hits the same small celebrity list, and any fan-out would flood the queue.
failures.fix: Celebrities are never fanned out. Replicate their hot list and cache the merged result for a few seconds.

failures.what: A deleted post is still in feeds
failures.impact: People see content that was removed, which can be harmful.
failures.fix: Do not chase every list. Mark the post deleted. When hydrating, drop deleted posts and fix the list lazily.

scaling.limit: Feed cache memory grows with users
scaling.lever: Shard lists by user id with consistent hashing, keep lists short, and evict inactive users.
Add workers, batch list updates per cache node, and lower the celebrity cutoff.
Run regional feed caches and replicate posts. Serve images from the CDN nearest the user.

recap.key: Reads outnumber posts, so precompute each feed. Push post ids to followers on write, but pull celebrities at read time.
recap.numbers: About 1K posts and 230K fan-out writes per second, 6K feed reads per second, and a few hundred GB of feed lists. One celebrity post is 10M writes.
moves: Estimate first: fan-out is posts per second times followers
Keep a cached id list per user, filled by queue workers
Hybrid: skip fan-out for celebrities and merge them on read
Rank in a separate stage, and filter deleted posts when hydrating
